c:count_publishers.why: IMPLEMENTED as of phase-381 W4, under our receiver: see `c:executor_count_publishers`. The previous text here said the whole family was absent -- "every one of those slots is NULL in every backend, nothing above them wraps a slot, and no C/C++/Rust entry point exists" -- which was true when written (phase-379 W3) and is not now. The zenoh backend fills the slot, the runtime wraps it and all three languages expose it.

c:executor_count_publishers.why: phase-381 W4. Same verb as ROS 2; the RECEIVER differs. ROS 2 hangs the graph off a node (`rcl_get_node_names(node, ...)`, `rclcpp::Node::get_node_names()`) because each Node/Context owns a participant. A nano-ros image opens ONE transport session for the whole image -- a session per node is RAM a 128 KiB target does not have -- and the Executor owns it, so the graph is asked of the Executor. Our `Node` is a declarative registration with no session to query. NOT a `rename`: renaming would say our spelling should change, and it should not -- the name follows the receiver, and the receiver is where the session is. The C spelling keeps the `nros_executor_*` infix every other session-scoped verb uses (`nros_executor_ping`, `nros_executor_spin`).

c:names_and_types_t.why: the result CARRIER, and its shape is decided against upstream's already. Every rcl graph call takes an `rcl_allocator_t *` and fills a two-level allocating array; there is no allocator at this seam (one global `nros_platform_alloc`) and the graph has no bound a CALLER can know, so a 128 KiB image would have to reserve permanently for the worst graph it might ever meet. `rmw_vtable.h` enumerates through VISITORS instead -- `rmw_node_visit_fn`, `rmw_names_and_types_visit_fn`, `rmw_topic_endpoint_info_visit_fn`, every string BORROWED for the call, peak extra RAM one entry, and a bounded caller stops early by returning `false` (a normal outcome, not a truncation error). Constraint: no allocator. So there is no array type to `init`/`fini` and there will not be one; what is missing is the QUERIES that would drive the visitor -- see `c:get_node_names`.

c:names_and_types_visit_fn.why: phase-381 W4. The ours-half of the `names_and_types_t` / `topic_endpoint_info_array_t` divergence already recorded in this file: upstream returns `rcutils_string_array_t` / `rmw_names_and_types_t`, which allocate two levels deep. There is no allocator at this seam, and a caller-provided buffer needs a bound the CALLER cannot know -- the graph has no such bound. So enumeration is a VISITOR: peak extra memory is one entry, the backend streams from state it already holds, every string is borrowed for the call, and a caller with its own limit stops early by returning false.

c:service_server_is_available.why: the theirs half of a name we already ship twice. rcl spells it `rcl_service_server_is_available(node, client, bool*)`; ours are `nros_client_server_available` and `nros_client_service_is_ready`, and service.json's `cpp:Client::service_is_ready` records the decision that `service_is_ready` is the name to keep (rclcpp and rclrs both use it) and `c:client_server_available` the one to drop. Recorded here as the rcl-side half so the pair is complete. CORRECTED 2026-08-27 (phase-379 W5): the previous text claimed "two real signature deviations ... no `node` parameter and no allocator". There is ONE. `rcl_service_server_is_available` takes no allocator either -- its three parameters are `(const rcl_node_t *node, const rcl_client_t *client, bool *is_available)`, verified in `docs/reference/api-surface/rclc.json` under `rcl/graph.h` -- so there was nothing to drop, and citing it as a deviation invented an alignment we already have. The real deviation is the missing `node`, and our ABI declares it in those words: `packages/core/nros-rmw-abi/include/nros/rmw_vtable.h:571`, "an image has no node object to pass -- the client reaches its session directly". Note the vtable SLOT already carries rcl's exact spelling -- `service_server_is_available(const rmw_client_t *, bool *out_available)` at :575 -- so the disagreement this row records is entirely in the public C/C++/Rust entry points ABOVE the vtable, not in the ABI. This is the ONE member of rcl's `graph.h` we implement (every other member reports `theirs-only`, verdicted `gap` or `divergence`), and it is implemented by exactly one backend: zenoh, via the session's liveliness subscription (`packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenoh/src/shim/service.rs:983`); Cyclone's slot is `nullptr` pending built-in topic readers (`packages/rmw/cyclonedds/nros-rmw-cyclonedds/src/vtable.cpp:98`), XRCE's is NULL for good (`packages/rmw/xrce/nros-rmw-xrce/src/vtable.c:80`).

rename.owner: c:client_server_available in service.json carries the edit — ONE decision, three rows
rename.resolution:
UNBLOCKED 2026-09-04. The previous `blocked-needs-decision` named `rust:ClientTrait::server_available` as its blocker; that row was DELETED on 2026-09-03 by 3941b569a when W6 decision 2 landed, and the tri-state question it waited on is answered — verified: the trait method is now `service_is_ready() -> Result<bool, _>` (`traits.rs:2849`). A status of "blocked" pointing at a row that no longer exists is worse than no status.

Nothing lands on this theirs-only key; it closes when the C swap executes.

c:topic_endpoint_info_array_t.why: the ARRAY of the above, which is the half that cannot survive: it is the allocated, caller-`fini`ed sequence the visitor exists to avoid. See `c:names_and_types_t`.

c:topic_endpoint_info_t.why: see `c:names_and_types_t` for the carrier argument. We DO have this record -- `rmw_topic_endpoint_info_t` in `rmw_entity.h`, field-for-field upstream's (node name, namespace, type, endpoint kind, gid, granted QoS) -- but with every string borrowed for the visit rather than allocated, and at the RMW seam rather than in the user header.

c:wait_for_publishers.why: blocks until at least N publishers are on a topic, or the timeout expires -- the startup-ordering primitive, one entity kind over from `nros_client_wait_for_service`, which we DO ship. So the pattern is already here (RFC-0021: the blocking helper takes the executor and drives it, which is what makes the timeout reliable on a single-threaded transport); what is missing is the count it would wait on. See `c:count_publishers`.

cpp:Event.why: `rclcpp::Event` is not a QoS event: it is `rclcpp/event.hpp`'s set/check flag, handed out by `Node::get_graph_event()` and waited on with `wait_for_graph_change()` -- a graph-change notification. It lands in this stage only because `topics.py` maps the `event` header stem to qos, which is right for `rcl/event.h` and wrong for this file. Declined for the graph stage's reason: static peers, no dynamic discovery, so there is no graph change to be notified of.

cpp:Event::Event.why: rclcpp's graph `Event` is a `shared_ptr`-held mutex+flag that a background graph LISTENER THREAD sets and `wait_for_graph_change` blocks on. Three constraints each rule the shape out: no allocator for the shared object (`make_shared` -- the same reason pubsub declines every `make_shared` factory), no background transport thread to run the listener (RFC-0002 puts one executor on one RTOS task and `rmw_vtable.h` says in its own words that no graph slot may block on the wire), and no blocking wait outside the executor (RFC-0021: a blocking helper takes the executor, as `nros_client_wait_for_service` does). Our shape for "the graph changed" is an EDGE: the `node_get_graph_guard_condition` slot, deliberately `set_wake_callback`-shaped rather than a waitable, carrying no payload because delivering WHAT changed means buffering it. That slot is NULL in every backend, so nothing fires today. What a user loses: no way to be told that a node or an endpoint appeared or went away -- only `nros_client_wait_for_service` / `Client::service_is_ready` answers that, and only for one service at a time. (CORRECTED 2026-09-04, phase-417: this cited `server_available`, which in C++ is now only a `[[deprecated]]` forwarder -- phase-379 W6 decision 2 settled the name as `service_is_ready`. C still exports both, which is what `c:client_server_available` records.) NOTE this contradicts the node stage's `c:node_get_graph_guard_condition`, which declines on "nothing would ever trigger it here"; the slot exists precisely so a backend CAN trigger it.

cpp:Event::make_shared.why: see `cpp:Event::Event`; a `shared_ptr` factory needs an allocator.

cpp:LifecycleNode::count_publishers.why:
LANDED 2026-09-04 (phase-417 stage 2b): `nros::Node` and `nros::LifecycleNode` now forward this to the executor that owns them (`node.hpp`, `lifecycle.hpp`), over FFI that already shipped on `nros::Executor` (`executor.hpp:205-301`). It was verdicted `gap` -- not implemented -- when the capability was present one type over and only the forwarder was missing.

It stays a divergence on SHAPE. rclcpp returns owned heap containers (`std::vector<std::string>`, `std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string>>`); the graph has no bound a caller can know, so a caller-sized buffer is an unanswerable question and an owned container needs an allocator. Ours streams through a visitor, which costs one entry of peak RAM.

ADOPT-BOUNDED envelope (RFC-0089), stated in the header: the call reports what has been DISCOVERED and never blocks, so an empty result means "nobody seen yet", not "nobody exists"; a backend with no graph returns `Unsupported`, which is a different answer from empty and must not be collapsed into zero.

rust:Executor::count_publishers.why: phase-381 W4. Same verb as ROS 2; the RECEIVER differs. ROS 2 hangs the graph off a node (`rcl_get_node_names(node, ...)`, `rclcpp::Node::get_node_names()`) because each Node/Context owns a participant. A nano-ros image opens ONE transport session for the whole image -- a session per node is RAM a 128 KiB target does not have -- and the Executor owns it, so the graph is asked of the Executor. Our `Node` is a declarative registration with no session to query. NOT a `rename`: renaming would say our spelling should change, and it should not -- the name follows the receiver, and the receiver is where the session is. The C spelling keeps the `nros_executor_*` infix every other session-scoped verb uses (`nros_executor_ping`, `nros_executor_spin`).

The GID is held by value and does survive a copy. (2) NO QoS ACCESSOR, deliberately, and absent rather than present-and-empty: rclcpp's `qos_profile()` reports the GRANTED profile, no backend behind this API can read a remote's grant back, and zenoh's liveliness token carries the DECLARING side's request rather than a negotiated grant -- so a ported file that asks for it fails to COMPILE instead of reading a QoS nobody granted (RFC-0089: never compile and differ).
